**SUBJECTIVE:**

* **Chief Complaint:** Joint pain in both knees, especially after moving boxes.
* **History of Present Illness (HPI):** The patient, a 62-year-old male, presents with complaints of joint pain in both knees, which started over the weekend after moving boxes up and down the basement stairs. The pain is described as a dull, aching sensation, especially with weight-bearing and movement. The patient reports that both knees are equally painful and that the pain has been persistent, even keeping him up at night.

**OBJECTIVE:**

* **Physical Examination & Vitals:** Not performed during this visit.
* **Diagnostic Results & Labs:** X-ray of the right knee: good bony alignment, no acute fracture.

**ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:**

* **Diagnoses and Clinical Reasoning:** Based on the patient's symptoms and medical history, it is likely that the patient is experiencing an acute exacerbation of his arthritis, possibly triggered by the physical strain of moving boxes. The patient's history of kidney transplant and arthritis may also be contributing factors.
* **Treatment Plan, Medications, and Follow-up:** The patient will be prescribed Ultram 50 mg every 6 hours as needed to manage his knee pain. An autoimmune panel will be ordered to further evaluate the patient's arthritis. The patient will be advised to rest his knees and avoid activities that exacerbate the pain. Follow-up will be scheduled in 2 weeks to reassess the patient's symptoms and adjust treatment as needed.

Please note that this is a sample SOAP note, and actual clinical notes may vary depending on the specific patient, provider, and healthcare setting.

They've been really sore and it even kept me up some on Saturday night. Doctor: Could you please describe the onset, duration, and any specific activities that make the knee pain worse? Patient: The pain started over the weekend when we were moving boxes up and down the basement stairs. It got worse as the day went on, and by the end of the day, my knees were killing me. Both knees are equally painful, and it's been pretty sore ever since. It even kept me up a bit on Saturday night. Doctor: Have you experienced any swelling, redness, or warmth in your knees? Have you had any previous injuries or surgeries to your knees? Do you have a history of arthritis or joint issues? Patient: I haven't noticed any swelling or redness, but my knees do feel tender to the touch. I've had some knee problems in the past, but nothing serious. I also have arthritis, which I've been dealing with for a while. Doctor: Could you describe the nature of the knee pain (e.g., sharp, dull, throbbing) and whether there are any factors that alleviate the pain? Patient: The pain is more of a dull, aching sensation, especially when I put weight on them. I tried taking some Tylenol and icing them, but nothing really helped. It's just been sore all day and kept me up a bit on Saturday night. Doctor: Could you please describe any specific movements or activities that make the pain better or worse? Have you noticed any clicking, locking, or instability in the knees? Patient: The pain gets worse when I put weight on them or try to move around a lot, like when I was moving boxes. It doesn't really get better with rest,

subjective.unit: Chief Complaint: Lower back pain
subjective.citation_text: Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today? Patient: I'm 55 years old, male, and I'm here because I've been having some back pain. It started about five days ago when I was helping my wife move a refrigerator and felt something in my lower right back. I'm just worried that maybe something happened, especially since I had a discectomy before. Doctor: Can you describe the nature of the back pain, whether it radiates to other areas, and if you have any associated symptoms such as numbness, tingling, or weakness in your legs? Patient: The pain is in my lower right back, and it hurts when I bend over. I haven't had any numbness, tingling, or weakness in my legs, just the pain in my back. Doctor: Could you describe the intensity of the pain on a scale from 1 to 10, and have you noticed any specific activities or positions that make the pain better or worse? Patient: The pain is a 6 or 7 out of 10. It feels worse when I bend over or try to move the way I did when I hurt it, but it doesn't get better much when I rest. Just the pain in my back, nothing else. Doctor: Could you describe any specific activities or movements that make the pain better or worse? Also, have you tried any treatments or interventions for the previous discectomy that might be relevant here? Patient: The pain is worse when I bend over or try to move the way I did when I hurt it, but it doesn't get better much when I rest. I've been taking ibuprofen and once tried Tylenol and ibuprofen together, which gave me some relief. I had a discectomy before, but I don't know if that's related to this. Doctor: Could you describe the specific location of the tenderness in your lower back and whether there is any radiating pain? Additionally, have you noticed any changes in your bowel or bladder function since the onset of the pain? Patient: The tenderness

Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today?
Patient: I'm 59 years old, male, and I'm here for a routine follow-up of my chronic problems. I've been dealing with depression, asthma, and diabetes, and I wanted to check in on how everything's been going.
Doctor: Could you please provide more details about your current symptoms or concerns related to your depression, asthma, or diabetes?
Patient: Sure. My depression has been kind of persistent, and I've been having some ups and downs with it. I've been weening myself off my medication, Prozac, because I felt some side effects, but I'm willing to try something else if needed. As for my asthma, it's been acting up a bit more this season because of the pollen, and I've been using my inhaler more when it's hot. I did feel a little lightheaded and dizzy the other day, but I thought it was just the heat. My diabetes has been manageable, but I did slip a bit with my diet over the weekend because we were traveling for sports tournaments and eating on the go. I'm trying to get back on track with my diet and monitoring my blood sugars.
Doctor: Could you provide details about the specific side effects you experienced with Prozac and whether you have consulted with your psychiatrist about tapering off the medication?
Patient: I didn't really talk to my psychiatrist about tapering off; I just kind of did it myself because I felt like I was starting to feel better, but now I'm realizing I might need to get back on something or try a different medication. The side effects were more like feeling a bit sluggish or having some stomach discomfort, but nothing too severe.
Doctor: Has the patient experienced any changes in his diabetes management plan, such as adjustments in insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents, since the slip in diet control?
Patient: No, I haven't made any changes to my diabetes management plan since the slip in diet control. I'm still on my regular medication, but I know my blood sugars might have been a bit higher lately because of the weekend food choices. I'm trying to get back on track with my diet and monitoring my blood sugars more closely at home.
Doctor: Could you please share more about how you're feeling emotionally lately, and whether you've noticed any changes in your mood or sleep patterns since you started tapering off Prozac?
Patient: Emotionally, I've been going through some ups and downs. I feel like I'm managing, but there are days when it's harder than others. I haven't really noticed a big change in my sleep patterns, but I do feel more fatigued than usual, which I think is partly from the stress of everything going on with the kids' tournaments and my health issues.
Doctor: Has the patient experienced any recent episodes of hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia since the dietary slip, and has he been monitoring his blood glucose levels more frequently as mentioned?
Patient: No, I haven't had any episodes of hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia since the dietary slip, but I have been monitoring my blood glucose levels more frequently at home to keep track of how I'm doing. I know I need to be more consistent with my diet and medication to keep my diabetes under control.
Doctor: Could you provide more details about the specific environmental triggers for your asthma symptoms, such as the types of pollen or specific heat-related conditions you are exposed to?
Patient: The specific environmental triggers for my asthma symptoms are mainly the pollen during the high pollen season, and when it's really hot, over 85 degrees, I start to feel it more. I've been using my inhaler more on those days, but I try to avoid being outside too much when it's that hot.
Doctor: Has the patient experienced any recent exacerbations of asthma symptoms requiring additional medication or emergency care?
Patient: No, I haven't had any recent exacerbations of my asthma symptoms that required additional medication or emergency care. I've been using my inhaler as needed, especially on hot days, but nothing too bad. I try to manage it by staying inside when it's really hot and avoiding the pollen as much as I can.
Doctor: Are you currently considering a specific antidepressant to replace Prozac, and have you discussed this with your psychiatrist or primary care provider?
Patient: I'm open to trying something different, like Zoloft, but I haven't really discussed it in detail with my psychiatrist yet. I just mentioned it to the doctor here, so I guess we can explore that option together. I'm willing to try it if it works better for me.
Doctor: Thank you for sharing that. It's important to work with your psychiatrist to make any changes to your antidepressant medication. Have you experienced any changes in your mood or energy levels since you tapered off Prozac?
Patient: I think my mood has been a bit more unstable since I tapered off Prozac, and I do feel more tired than usual. It's been harder to stay motivated, but I'm trying to stay positive and manage it the best I can.
Doctor: Could you tell me more about how your mood has been fluctuating since you tapered off Prozac? Have you noticed any specific triggers or patterns to these emotional ups and downs?
Patient: I think my mood has been a bit more unstable since I tapered off Prozac, and I do feel more tired than usual. It's been harder to stay motivated, but I'm trying to stay positive and manage it the best I can.
Doctor: Could you tell me more about how your fatigue is affecting your daily activities and whether you've noticed any changes in your mood patterns over the past few weeks?
Patient: The fatigue has been making it harder to get through my day, especially with all the running up and down stairs or lifting things. I feel like I have less energy to keep up with everything, and my mood seems to dip more often, especially when I'm tired. I haven't really noticed a specific pattern, but it feels like the tiredness makes the depression feel worse.
Doctor: Thank you for sharing that. I understand how challenging it can be to manage fatigue and mood changes. To better support you, could you tell me if you've noticed any specific times of day when your fatigue is worse, or if there are any activities that seem to make it better or worse?
Patient: The fatigue is worst in the afternoons, and it feels like it gets worse when I'm doing physical tasks, like lifting boxes or running up stairs. It doesn't really get better with rest, but I do feel a little better in the mornings after I ride my bike. I guess the physical activity helps a bit, but it's not enough to really fight the tiredness all day.
Doctor: Could you tell me more about how your mood has been affected by the fatigue? Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or motivation since the fatigue started?
Patient: My appetite hasn't really changed much, but I do feel less motivated to do things, especially when I'm tired. It's like the fatigue takes away some of my drive, and I just don't feel like pushing through as much as I used to.
Doctor: Has the patient experienced any changes in his thyroid function tests recently, or is there a history of thyroid disorders?
Patient: I don't know about any changes in thyroid function tests or a history of thyroid disorders. That information isn't available to me.

retained.atom: There is some bruising on the back side of the leg.
retained.citation: Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today? Patient: Hello. I'm 43 years old, and I'm here because I hurt the top part of my right leg. I was bowling, and I accidentally hit my leg with the ball instead of the lane, and then I fell. It's been sore ever since. Doctor: Could you please provide your gender and describe the nature of the pain in your right leg, including when it started and if there is any swelling, bruising, or difficulty moving the leg? Patient: I'm female. The pain started when I hit my leg with the bowling ball, and it's been sore ever since. There's a little bruising on the back side of my leg, and it's swollen a little, but not too much. It's hard to walk on it, and I'm careful not to put too much weight on it. Doctor: Have you experienced any numbness, tingling, or weakness in your right leg since the injury? Patient: No, I haven't had any numbness, tingling, or weakness in my right leg since the injury. It's just sore and bruised, and I'm careful not to put too much weight on it. Doctor: Have you had any prior injuries or surgeries to your right leg, and do you have any known medical conditions such as diabetes, osteoporosis, or blood clotting disorders? Patient: No, I haven't had any prior injuries or surgeries to my right leg. I do have a history of atopic eczema, and I had a colectomy in the past due to diverticulitis, but that was on my abdomen, not my leg. I don't have diabetes, osteoporosis, or any blood clotting disorders that I'm aware of. Doctor: Could you describe the exact location of the pain on your right leg and whether you've noticed any deformity or instability in the area? Patient: The pain is on the top part of my right leg, more on the side.

Patient: I have chronic congestive heart failure with diastolic dysfunction. I was on furosemide before, but they switched me to torsemide 20 milligrams by mouth daily. Doctor: Could you describe the current pain level in your right knee and how it affects your daily activities? Patient: My knee pain is manageable most of the time, but it does bother me when I try to walk longer distances or go up and down stairs. It's been making it harder to keep up with my gardening, which I really enjoy. I'm hoping the surgery will help me get back to doing more of the things I love. Doctor: Could you please provide the results of your most recent echocardiogram, blood pressure readings, and any recent laboratory tests such as BNP or electrolyte levels? Additionally, could you share the findings from your physical examination and any imaging or lab tests related to your knee condition? Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today?
Patient: I'm 86 years old, and I'm a male. I'm here because I've been having pain in my left arm, especially at night, and it's been going on for about two weeks. It started suddenly one morning and has been bothering me on and off since.
Doctor: Can you describe the nature of the arm pain (e.g., sharp, dull, throbbing)? Does it radiate to other areas? Have you experienced any associated symptoms such as chest pain, shortness of breath, numbness, or tingling? Additionally, have you had any prior history of similar episodes or any known medical conditions such as hypertension, diabetes, or coronary artery disease?
Patient: The pain is more of a dull ache, but it can feel sharp at times, especially when I move my hand. It starts in my hand and goes all the way down my arm. I haven't had any chest pain or shortness of breath, but I do have some numbness and tingling in my hand. I also have neuropathy in this finger from an old injury, and I'm one percent disabled from leg issues. I don't have diabetes or heart problems, as far as I know.
Doctor: Have you undergone any prior cardiac evaluations, such as an electrocardiogram (ECG), echocardiogram, or stress test? If so, please provide the results or dates of these tests.
Patient: I don't recall having any heart tests done, to be honest. I've been focused on the arm pain and the issues with my leg, which is why I was referred here. I don't think I've had an ECG or anything like that before.
Doctor: Have you undergone any recent imaging studies, such as an X-ray, MRI, or CT scan of the arm, neck, or chest? If so, please provide the results or details of those examinations.
Patient: I don't recall having any recent imaging done on my arm or neck, but I was told I have arthritis in my neck from an X-ray. I haven't had an MRI yet, though.
Doctor: Have you experienced any recent trauma or injury to your neck or arm that could be related to the current symptoms?
Patient: No, I don't recall any recent trauma or injury to my neck or arm. The pain started suddenly one morning, and I don't remember anything happening to cause it. It just began hurting really bad, and I had to ice it to get some relief.
Doctor: Could you please describe the exact location of the pain in your left arm and hand, and whether it is accompanied by any weakness or changes in sensation, such as numbness or tingling, in specific areas?
Patient: The pain starts in my hand and goes all the way down my arm. I have some numbness and tingling in my hand, and I notice weakness when I try to grip things. My finger, which I hurt a while back, doesn't work properly either.
Doctor: Could you please provide details about any neurological deficits you are experiencing, such as weakness, numbness, or tingling in other parts of your body, and whether you have any history of cardiac issues or risk factors like hypertension, hyperlipidemia, or smoking?
Patient: I don't have any weakness, numbness, or tingling in other parts of my body besides my hand and that one finger. As far as I know, I don't have any heart issues or risk factors like high blood pressure or high cholesterol. I don't smoke, either.
Doctor: Could you please describe the current physical examination findings, including your vital signs and any neurological assessment of your upper extremity that has been performed?
Patient: I don't have the details of a physical exam done by another doctor, but when Dr. Miller examined me, he had me do some movements with my arms and checked my reflexes. He said my reflexes were all negative, and he didn't find any tenderness in my neck. He also had me squeeze his fingers to check my strength, and it felt about the same in both hands.
Doctor: Could you provide the results of the nerve conduction studies, imaging (such as MRI of the cervical spine), and ECG that are pending?
Patient: I don't have the results of any nerve conduction studies, MRI of my cervical spine, or ECG yet. Those tests are still pending, and I'm waiting to see what they show.

Doctor: Thank you for letting me know the test results are still pending. I understand this can be concerning while waiting for the results. Once we have the ECG, nerve conduction studies, and MRI of the cervical spine, we will be able to better understand the cause of your symptoms. In the meantime, is there anything else you would like to share about your symptoms or concerns?
Patient: In the meantime, I don't have anything else to share about my symptoms. The pain in my left arm still comes and goes, especially at night, and I've noticed some weakness in my hand when gripping things. I'm just hoping the tests will help us figure out what's going on and how to make it better.
Doctor: Thank you for sharing that with me. I understand that the pain and weakness can be concerning. To better understand your condition, could you let me know if you've experienced any similar symptoms in the past or if there are any other factors that might be contributing to your discomfort?

Doctor: Have you undergone any recent echocardiograms or other cardiac imaging studies to assess the function of your aortic valve or the status of your ascending aorta? Patient: Yes, I had an echocardiogram recently, but I'm not sure exactly when. I think it was around September 2019, and I was told that everything looked okay. Doctor: Could you please provide the specific results of your September 2019 echocardiogram, particularly regarding the aortic valve function and the size of your ascending aorta? Patient: I don't have the specific results of the September 2019 echocardiogram with me, but I was told that everything looked okay at the time. Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today?
Patient: I'm 76 years old, and I'm a female. I'm here to establish care with you because I had a lumpectomy last year for ductal carcinoma in situ in my right breast. I'm feeling good overall, but I want to make sure I'm being properly followed up on.
Doctor: Could you please provide your height, weight, and any current medications or supplements you are taking?
Patient: I'm 76 years old, and I'm a female. I'm here to establish care with you because I had a lumpectomy last year for ductal carcinoma in situ in my right breast. I'm feeling good overall, but I want to make sure I'm being properly followed up on.
Doctor: Could you please provide details about your current medications, supplements, and any symptoms or concerns related to your past history of ductal carcinoma in situ?
Patient: I take coq10, vitamin d, vitamin c, fish oil, and elderberry fruit. I don't have any symptoms related to my past history, and I'm feeling good overall. I do have some back and knee pain, which my doctors say is age-related, and I've been working on lowering my cholesterol through diet and exercise.
Doctor: Please describe the nature, duration, and severity of your back and knee pain, including any factors that aggravate or relieve it.
Patient: The back pain is more of a constant ache, especially in the lower back, and it's been going on for a few years. It gets worse when I stand for long periods or lift things, but it feels a little better when I rest or stretch. The knee pain is similar—mostly in my left knee, and it bothers me when I walk or go up stairs, but I can manage it with some rest.
Doctor: Could you please provide the results of any recent imaging or laboratory tests related to your breast cancer follow-up or the back and knee pain?
Patient: I don't have any recent imaging or lab tests specifically for my back and knee pain, but my last mammogram in January 2021 was normal and showed no signs of recurrence. My primary care doctor is managing my back and knee pain, and they've said it's related to aging. I haven't had any other tests for those issues recently.
Doctor: Could you please confirm if you have any other medical conditions or medications that you are currently taking, and if you have had any recent physical examinations or tests?
Patient: I don't have any other medical conditions besides high cholesterol, which I'm managing through diet and exercise. I take coq10, vitamin d, vitamin c, fish oil, and elderberry fruit, and that's all. I had a physical examination with you today, and my last mammogram was in January 2021, which was normal. I haven't had any other recent tests or exams.
Doctor: Could you please describe any recent changes in your back or knee pain, and whether your current management strategies, such as rest or stretching, have been effective in managing your symptoms?
Patient: The back pain hasn't really changed much—it's still there, but I manage it with rest and stretching. The knee pain is the same, too. I can walk and go up stairs, but it does bother me a bit. I haven't needed any medication for it, and I'm trying to stay active as much as I can.
Doctor: Thank you for sharing that. To ensure we have a complete understanding of your health, could you please tell me if you have any known allergies or have experienced any other symptoms besides the back and knee pain?
Patient: I don't have any known allergies besides penicillin. Other than the back and knee pain, I haven't had any other symptoms or issues recently. I feel generally well and am managing my cholesterol through diet and exercise.
Doctor: Could you please share any recent imaging or lab tests you've had for your back and knee pain, if available?
Patient: I don't have any recent imaging or lab tests specifically for my back and knee pain. My primary care doctor is managing those issues and has said they're related to aging. I haven't had any other tests for those problems recently.
Doctor: Could you please confirm if there are any other symptoms or concerns you would like to discuss during this visit?
Patient: I don't have any other symptoms or concerns to discuss right now. I'm feeling well overall, and I'm happy with the plan to come back in a year after my mammogram in April 2022. Everything seems under control.

**SUBJECTIVE:**

* **Chief Complaint:** Pain in the right hip, especially in the groin area, with a catching or grabbing sensation.
* **History of Present Illness (HPI):** The patient, a 56-year-old woman, presents with a 2-year history of pain in the right hip, particularly in the groin area. The pain is described as a grabbing or catching sensation, especially when pivoting or moving quickly. The patient reports a 2-7 out of 10 pain level, with occasional episodes of near-falling. She has experienced weight loss of 110 pounds through Weight Watchers, which has helped decrease some of the pain.

**OBJECTIVE:**

* **Physical Examination & Vitals:** Not mentioned.
* **Diagnostic Results & Labs:**
	+ MRI arthrogram of the right hip (June 3rd, 2021): High-grade chondromalacia involving the interosseous superior right acetabulum with subchondral marrow edema and cyst formation.

* **Diagnoses and Clinical Reasoning:** Based on the patient's symptoms and diagnostic results, it is likely that the patient has degenerative joint disease in the right hip, which is contributing to the pain, catching sensation, and limited range of motion.
* **Treatment Plan, Medications, and Follow-up:** The patient will be referred to an orthopedic specialist for further evaluation and management. In the meantime, she will be advised to continue managing her pain with non-pharmacological methods and to avoid activities that exacerbate the condition. Follow-up appointments will be scheduled to monitor the patient's progress and adjust the treatment plan as needed.

reference_so.subjective:
Basic information: 56-year-old female presenting with right hip pain since February 2020, localized to the groin area, with episodes of catching and near-fall incidents.

History of present illness: The pain is described as a grabbing or catching feeling, especially when pivoting or moving certain ways. It ranges from about 2 to 7 out of 10 in intensity and does not radiate elsewhere—it remains localized to the groin area. The episodes occur intermittently, sometimes several times in a row, and other times not at all. The patient reports stiffness and limited range of motion in the right hip, particularly during pivoting movements. She experiences episodes of catching and near-fall incidents, which affect her mobility and daily activities. The patient has experienced consistent symptoms over the past year, with some pain reduction due to weight loss but persistent catching sensations. The catching episodes seem to happen more when she pivots or moves quickly, like turning her body or stepping back. It can happen anywhere, not just during a specific activity. Over the past year, the pain has been somewhat consistent, ranging from a 2 to a 7 out of 10, and it still happens several times in a row sometimes, though it doesn’t always happen. The weight loss has helped decrease some of the pain, but the catching sensation is still there.

Past history: The patient has a history of PCL surgery, infertility treatments, and cholecystectomy. She has experienced significant weight loss (110 pounds) through Weight Watchers, which has been maintained for over a year. No recent hip-related surgeries or trauma reported.
reference_so.objective:
Physical examination: The patient reports stiffness and limited range of motion in the right hip, particularly during pivoting movements. She experiences episodes of catching and near-fall incidents, which affect her mobility and daily activities. There is no mention of fever, chills, or radiation of pain beyond the groin area. The patient denies any swelling, redness, or warmth in the right hip area. She does not have morning stiffness or stiffness after being inactive for a while—it doesn’t last more than a few minutes, if at all.

Investigations: MRI arthrogram of the right hip on June 3rd, 2021, showed high-grade chondromalacia involving the interosseous superior right acetabulum with subchondral marrow edema and cyst formation, consistent with degenerative joint disease.

My ankles have been swelling, and I've been having a hard time breathing, especially at night. I had to call an ambulance and was taken to the hospital for heart failure. Doctor: Could you please provide more details about the duration and progression of your swelling and shortness of breath? Have you experienced any other symptoms such as fatigue, chest pain, or palpitations? Additionally, have you been diagnosed with heart failure before, and if so, what medications are you currently taking? Patient: I haven't been diagnosed with heart failure before, but I was told I was in the hospital for it. I was having trouble with my ankles swelling and couldn't get them to go down, even when I was in bed. I had to prop myself up to breathe at night, and I felt really bad. I called 911 because I was having a hard time talking, and they took me to the ER. I was told my blood pressure was really high, like 200 over 90. I try to take my medications, but I might miss a dose now and then. I also eat a lot of salty foods, like salt and vinegar potato chips, which I snack on every day at home. Doctor: Have you been evaluated for kidney function or tested for proteinuria, such as a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio or a 24-hour urine protein test, since your hospitalization for heart failure? Patient: I don't know if I've had any tests for kidney function or proteinuria since I was in the hospital. I wasn't told about any of those specific tests, but I do know I have some kidney disease, which the doctor mentioned. Doctor: Could you confirm if you were told about any kidney function tests, such as serum creatinine or eGFR, or any urine tests for proteinuria, like the urine albumin-to-creatinine

Doctor: Could you please provide more details about the duration and progression of your swelling and shortness of breath? Have you experienced any other symptoms such as fatigue, chest pain, or palpitations? Additionally, have you been diagnosed with heart failure before, and if so, what medications are you currently taking? Patient: I haven't been diagnosed with heart failure before, but I was told I was in the hospital for it. I was having trouble with my ankles swelling and couldn't get them to go down, even when I was in bed. I had to prop myself up to breathe at night, and I felt really bad. I called 911 because I was having a hard time talking, and they took me to the ER. I was told my blood pressure was really high, like 200 over 90. I try to take my medications, but I might miss a dose now and then. I also eat a lot of salty foods, like salt and vinegar potato chips, which I snack on every day at home. Doctor: Have you been evaluated for kidney function or tested for proteinuria, such as a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio or a 24-hour urine protein test, since your hospitalization for heart failure? Patient: I don't know if I've had any tests for kidney function or proteinuria since I was in the hospital. I wasn't told about any of those specific tests, but I do know I have some kidney disease, which the doctor mentioned. Doctor: Could you confirm if you were told about any kidney function tests, such as serum creatinine or eGFR, or any urine tests for proteinuria, like the urine albumin-to-creatinine

subjective.unit: Chief Complaint: Pain in both elbows, especially the right one, for about 1.5 years.
subjective.citation_text: Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today? Patient: I'm 32, male. I've been having a lot of pain in both of my elbows, especially the right one. It's been going on for about a year and a half, and it really hurts when I use my arms or hands a lot. I've been taking ibuprofen, but it hasn't helped much. Doctor: Can you describe the nature of the pain in your elbows (e.g., sharp, dull, throbbing)? Have you noticed any swelling, stiffness, or numbness in the affected areas? Additionally, have you had any prior injuries or treatments for your elbows? Patient: The pain is more of a dull ache, especially on the inside of my right elbow. It really flares up when I use my arms or hands a lot, like lifting weights. I haven’t had any swelling or numbness, just the pain. I haven’t had any prior injuries to my elbows, just this new issue that started about a year and a half ago. Doctor: Have you undergone any previous imaging or consultations for this elbow pain? If so, please provide details. Patient: No, I haven't had any imaging or consultations for this before. This is the first time I'm really seeing a doctor about it. I just kept taking ibuprofen and hoping it would get better, but it hasn't. Doctor: Have you experienced any repetitive strain or occupational activities that involve repetitive elbow movements, such as weightlifting, typing, or manual labor? Additionally, do you have a family history of joint or autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis? Patient: I lift a lot of weights, like pretty heavy ones, and I've been doing that for a while. I don't think there's any family history of joint issues or arthritis that I'm aware of. Doctor: Have you experienced any stiffness, clicking, or locking in your elbows, and if so, how often does this occur? Patient: No,

Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today?
Patient: I'm 32, male. I've been having a lot of pain in both of my elbows, especially the right one. It's been going on for about a year and a half, and it really hurts when I use my arms or hands a lot. I've been taking ibuprofen, but it hasn't helped much.
Doctor: Can you describe the nature of the pain in your elbows (e.g., sharp, dull, throbbing)? Have you noticed any swelling, stiffness, or numbness in the affected areas? Additionally, have you had any prior injuries or treatments for your elbows?
Patient: The pain is more of a dull ache, especially on the inside of my right elbow. It really flares up when I use my arms or hands a lot, like lifting weights. I haven’t had any swelling or numbness, just the pain. I haven’t had any prior injuries to my elbows, just this new issue that started about a year and a half ago.
Doctor: Have you undergone any previous imaging or consultations for this elbow pain? If so, please provide details.
Patient: No, I haven't had any imaging or consultations for this before. This is the first time I'm really seeing a doctor about it. I just kept taking ibuprofen and hoping it would get better, but it hasn't.
Doctor: Have you experienced any repetitive strain or occupational activities that involve repetitive elbow movements, such as weightlifting, typing, or manual labor? Additionally, do you have a family history of joint or autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis?
Patient: I lift a lot of weights, like pretty heavy ones, and I've been doing that for a while. I don't think there's any family history of joint issues or arthritis that I'm aware of.
Doctor: Have you experienced any stiffness, clicking, or locking in your elbows, and if so, how often does this occur?
Patient: No, I haven't experienced any stiffness, clicking, or locking in my elbows. It's just the pain, especially on the inside of my right elbow, that's been bothering me a lot. It flares up when I use my arms or hands a lot, like when I'm lifting weights.
Doctor: Have you noticed any swelling, redness, or warmth in your elbows?
Patient: No, I haven't noticed any swelling, redness, or warmth in my elbows. It's just the pain, especially on the inside of my right elbow, that's been bothering me a lot. It flares up when I use my arms or hands a lot, like when I'm lifting weights.
Doctor: Could you describe the specific type of weightlifting you perform, including the frequency, duration, and any recent changes in your routine? Additionally, have you noticed any tenderness or localized swelling on the inside of your right elbow during or after weightlifting?
Patient: I mainly do bench presses, deadlifts, and overhead presses, a few times a week. I haven't changed my routine much, but I do lift pretty heavy. I definitely feel tenderness on the inside of my right elbow, especially after a workout, but no swelling. It just aches a lot afterward.
Doctor: Have you experienced any numbness, tingling, or weakness in your hands or fingers, especially on the side of the affected elbow?
Patient: No, I haven't experienced any numbness, tingling, or weakness in my hands or fingers. My hands feel normal, and I haven't noticed any issues with grip strength or sensation. It's just the pain on the inside of my elbow that's been bothering me.
Doctor: Have you undergone any previous imaging studies, such as X-rays or MRI scans, of your elbows? If so, could you provide details about the findings or the reason for the imaging?
Patient: No, I haven't had any imaging studies of my elbows before. The doctor just mentioned taking some X-rays when I came in, and they didn't show any fractures or bone issues, but they want to do an MRI next to get a better look. I didn't know anything about that before today.
Doctor: Could you describe the exact location of the tenderness on the inside of your right elbow? Is it near the medial epicondyle or more distal? Additionally, have you noticed any changes in the intensity or frequency of the pain over the past 1.5 years?
Patient: The tenderness is right on the inside of my elbow, near where the bone kind of sticks out. It’s definitely around the medial epicondyle area. The pain has been pretty consistent over the past year and a half, but it’s gotten worse as I keep lifting. It doesn’t really come and go—it just aches more the more I use my arms.
Doctor: Have you been evaluated by a rheumatologist or orthopedic specialist for this elbow pain, and have you had any blood tests to check for inflammatory or autoimmune conditions?
Patient: No, I haven't been evaluated by a rheumatologist or orthopedic specialist for this yet. The doctor today mentioned sending me for an MRI, but I haven't had any blood tests or other specialist visits. I didn't even know I needed to see someone else for this.
Doctor: Have you had any blood tests to check for inflammatory markers such as ESR or CRP, or autoimmune conditions like rheumatoid arthritis?
Patient: No, I haven't had any blood tests for inflammatory markers or autoimmune conditions. I didn't even know I needed them until today. The doctor just mentioned the MRI and this whole blood transfusion thing, so I'm still trying to wrap my head around everything.
Doctor: Could you describe the exact location of the tenderness in your right elbow? Also, have you noticed any changes in the pattern or intensity of the pain over the past 1.5 years?
Patient: The tenderness is right on the inside of my elbow, near the medial epicondyle, where the bone kind of sticks out. The pain has been pretty consistent over the past year and a half, but it’s gotten worse as I keep lifting weights. It doesn’t really come and go—it just aches more the more I use my arms.
Doctor: Have you had any prior imaging or blood tests for the elbows or related conditions, and if so, what were the results?
Patient: No, I haven't had any prior imaging or blood tests for my elbows or related conditions. The doctor just mentioned taking some X-rays when I came in, and they didn't show any fractures or bone issues, but they want to do an MRI next to get a better look. I didn't know anything about that before today.
Doctor: Could you describe the exact location of the tenderness on your right elbow and whether the pain radiates to any other part of your arm? Additionally, have you noticed any changes in the pattern or intensity of the pain over the past 1.5 years?
Patient: The tenderness is right on the inside of my elbow, near the medial epicondyle, where the bone sticks out. The pain doesn’t really radiate anywhere else—it just stays in that area. Over the past year and a half, it’s gotten worse as I keep lifting weights, and it aches more the more I use my arms. It’s been pretty consistent, though, no real changes in how it feels other than it getting more uncomfortable over time.

I'm here because I've had a sore throat for about four days, and I think I had a fever last night. I was really sweaty, but I didn't check my temperature because I was already in bed. Have you noticed any other symptoms such as cough, runny nose, or difficulty breathing? Patient: I'm 45 and female. My sore throat has been going on for about four days, and it's really bad—every time I swallow, it hurts, and it's even hard to eat. I haven't had a cough, but I do have a stuffy nose, and I was having chills and a lot of sweating last night. I didn't check my temperature, though. Doctor: Have you experienced any recent travel, close contact with individuals who have infectious diseases, or exposure to sick individuals? Patient: No, I haven't traveled recently, and I don't think I've been in close contact with anyone who's sick. My kids go to school, and they always have little colds or coughs, but nobody else in the house is really complaining of anything. Doctor: Could you please describe whether your sore throat is on one side (unilateral) or both sides (bilateral), and whether you notice any white patches or pus on your tonsils? Patient: It's on both sides, and I think my tonsils are swollen. I don't know if there's white stuff on them, but I do notice some kind of discharge when I look in the mirror. subjective.unit: Chief Complaint: Ready to quit smoking
subjective.citation_text: Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today? Patient: I'm 44 years old, and I'm here because I'm ready to quit smoking. I've been trying, but it's been really hard, and I wanted some help and support. Doctor: Could you please confirm your gender and let me know if you have any other concerns or symptoms you'd like to discuss today? Patient: I'm male, and I don't have any other concerns or symptoms besides wanting to quit smoking. I just need support and guidance to help me succeed this time. Doctor: Can you tell me about your smoking history, including how long you've been smoking and how many cigarettes you typically smoke per day? Patient: I started smoking in high school, mostly experimenting with friends or at parties, and it gradually became more regular. Now, at 44, I smoke a pack and a half a day, and I usually have my first cigarette within an hour of waking up. Doctor: Can you tell me about any previous attempts you've made to quit smoking and what challenges you faced? Also, have you experienced any symptoms like coughing, shortness of breath, or fatigue that you'd like to discuss? Patient: I actually tried quitting cold turkey once before, and I did really well for almost a year until things got really stressful at work. That's when I started picking it up again. I haven't had any major symptoms like coughing or shortness of breath, but I know smoking isn't good for me, especially with my history of gout and diabetes. I'm really motivated now because I'm about to be a father, and I want to be there for my daughter. Doctor: Could you provide more details about your history of gout and diabetes, including when they were diagnosed, how they are currently managed, and whether they have been affected by your smoking habit? Patient: I was diagnosed with type two diabetes a few years back, and I manage it with diet and exercise.

subjective.citation_text: Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today? Patient: I'm 32 years old and female. I'm here because of this knee pain I've been having for about six months now. It's in both knees and it's been really affecting my ability to run, which I used to love doing. Doctor: Could you please describe the nature of the knee pain? Is it sharp, dull, aching, or burning? Does it worsen with certain activities or at specific times of the day? Patient: It's more of a deep achy pain, like right behind my kneecaps. It really hurts when I stand up from sitting for a while or when I go up and down the stairs. Doctor: Have you experienced any morning stiffness in your knees, and if so, how long does it last? Have you noticed any clicking, locking, or instability in your knees? Patient: No, I haven't had any morning stiffness in my knees. And I don't really notice any clicking, locking, or instability in my knees when I move them. It's just that deep ache, especially when I stand up or go up and down stairs. Doctor: Have you experienced any other joint pains or symptoms in other parts of your body, such as your hips, ankles, or fingers, over the past six months? Patient: No, I haven't had any other joint pains or symptoms

Doctor: Could you provide the exact size of the kidney stone identified on the CT scan, and have you been prescribed any medications for pain management or stone passage? Patient: I don't know the exact size of the stone, but my doctor mentioned it was about half a centimeter. reference_so.subjective:
Basic information: Mason, adult, referred by primary care doctor for kidney stones

History of present illness: Sudden right back pain radiating to groin one week ago, CT scan confirmed kidney stone, straining urine without visible stones. Patient described intense pain in the right back radiating to the groin, accompanied by sweating and nausea, but no vomiting or hematuria. No pain or burning when urinating, and no feeling of incomplete bladder emptying. Patient was prescribed oxycodone for pain and continues to take Tylenol for breakthrough pain. Patient reports pain has been mostly gone since the initial episode, with occasional brief recurrences. Patient has been increasing water intake to help pass the stone and does not track dietary intake closely, though he does not consume a lot of salt or protein.

Past history: No prior history of kidney stones reported. No relevant surgical history. No known allergies. No family history of kidney stones or urological conditions.

Doctor: Could you please provide your age, gender, and any other symptoms you may be experiencing along with the itchy scalp and dandruff? Patient: I'm Barbara, and I'm female. I'm not sure about my exact age, but I've been dealing with this for a while. Other than the itching and dandruff, I don't have any other symptoms like rashes on my body or joint pain, and I've been feeling pretty good otherwise. Doctor: Could you please provide more details about any treatments you have tried for your scalp condition, including over-the-counter or prescription medications, shampoos, or other remedies? Additionally, have you noticed any triggers or patterns related to the itching or dandruff? Patient: I've tried over-the-counter treatments like Head and Shoulders shampoo and even castor oil, but nothing has really helped. I don't use a lot of hair products, just dye my hair occasionally, which I've been doing for years. I haven't noticed any specific triggers, just that it's been getting worse over the past six months. Doctor: Can you describe the appearance of the dandruff? Is it white, yellowish, or oily? Patient: Hi, I'm Barbara. I'm here because I've been dealing with a really itchy scalp for a while now, and it's been getting worse over the past six months or so. It's pretty embarrassing because I have a lot of dandruff, and it's just constant itching.
Doctor: Could you please provide your age, gender, and any other symptoms you may be experiencing along with the itchy scalp and dandruff?
Patient: I'm Barbara, and I'm female. I'm not sure about my exact age, but I've been dealing with this for a while. Other than the itching and dandruff, I don't have any other symptoms like rashes on my body or joint pain, and I've been feeling pretty good otherwise.
Doctor: Could you please provide more details about any treatments you have tried for your scalp condition, including over-the-counter or prescription medications, shampoos, or other remedies? Additionally, have you noticed any triggers or patterns related to the itching or dandruff?
Patient: I've tried over-the-counter treatments like Head and Shoulders shampoo and even castor oil, but nothing has really helped. I don't use a lot of hair products, just dye my hair occasionally, which I've been doing for years. I haven't noticed any specific triggers, just that it's been getting worse over the past six months.
Doctor: Can you describe the appearance of the dandruff? Is it white, yellowish, or oily? Are there any areas of redness, scaling, or inflammation on your scalp?
Patient: The dandruff is mostly white, and there's a lot of it, especially on my clothes throughout the day. My scalp has these red, scaly patches, and they're pretty itchy. They're spread out across the back of my head.
Doctor: Have you noticed any changes in your hair texture or experienced any hair loss? Also, could you describe your current hair care routine and any potential allergens or irritants you may be exposed to?
Patient: I haven't noticed any changes in my hair texture or hair loss. My hair care routine is pretty simple—I just wash it regularly and dye it occasionally, which I've been doing for years. I don't use a lot of products, so I don't think I'm exposed to many irritants.
Doctor: Have you noticed any pain, swelling, or changes in the appearance of the red, scaly patches on your scalp over the past six months?
Patient: No, I haven't noticed any pain or swelling, and the red, scaly patches have just been there consistently over the past six months. They don't seem to be getting worse, but they're still really itchy and embarrassing.
Doctor: Have you had any recent changes in your hair care routine, such as new shampoos, conditioners, or hair dyes, that might have triggered or worsened the symptoms?
Patient: No, I haven't changed my hair care routine recently. I still just wash my hair regularly and dye it occasionally, which I've been doing for years. I don't use a lot of other products, so I don't think that's causing it to get worse.
Doctor: Has the patient undergone any previous skin or scalp biopsies, and if so, what were the findings?
Patient: I don't think I've ever had a biopsy done on my scalp before. I've just been dealing with this for so long and trying different treatments, but nothing has really worked.
Doctor: Have you had any recent changes in your diet, stress levels, or exposure to new environments that might be contributing to your symptoms?
Patient: No, I don't think so. My diet has stayed pretty much the same, and I haven't really had any big changes in my life or stress levels. I mean, it's been the same old stuff, so I don't think that's contributing to it.
Doctor: Have you ever had a scalp biopsy or any other skin tests done in the past? If so, what were the results?
Patient: I don't think I've ever had a biopsy done on my scalp before. I've just been dealing with this for so long and trying different treatments, but nothing has really worked.
Doctor: Have you ever been diagnosed with a skin condition such as psoriasis, eczema, or fungal infections in the past?
Patient: No, I don't think I've ever been officially diagnosed with anything like psoriasis, eczema, or a fungal infection before. I've just been using over-the-counter treatments and trying different things, but nothing has really helped. My sister mentioned she has a dry scalp, but nothing as bad as what I'm going through.
Doctor: Have you noticed any changes in your scalp condition in response to specific environmental factors, such as weather, humidity, or exposure to certain chemicals?
Patient: No, I don't think the weather or humidity has really made it better or worse. I haven't been exposed to any new chemicals either, just my regular hair dye, which I've been using for years. I don't think that's what's causing it to get worse.
Doctor: Has the patient ever been diagnosed with psoriasis, eczema, or a fungal infection, or has she undergone a scalp biopsy in the past?
Patient: No, I don't think I've ever been diagnosed with psoriasis, eczema, or a fungal infection before, and I don't think I've ever had a scalp biopsy done. I've just been dealing with this for so long and trying different treatments, but nothing has really worked.
Doctor: Have you noticed any changes in your scalp's appearance or symptoms in response to stress, dietary changes, or new medications?
Patient: No, I don't think stress, dietary changes, or new medications have really made a difference. It's been pretty much the same for a while now, and I haven't noticed any changes in how it looks or feels because of those things.
Doctor: Have you had any recent changes in your hair care routine, such as switching to a new shampoo or conditioner, or using any new hair products?
Patient: No, I haven't changed my hair care routine recently. I still use the same products I've been using for a while now, and I don't really use a lot of different hair products. The only thing I do is dye my hair, which I've been doing for years.

Doctor: Could you please provide your full name and any relevant family medical history? Patient: My name is Karen Nelson. I don't really know about family medical history, but my dad said there's no history of seizures in our family, and he didn't hear of anything like Tourette's before. Doctor: Can you describe the nature of the twitch in your right eye? For example, how often does it happen, how long does each twitch last, and is there anything that seems to trigger it? Patient: The twitch happens a few times an hour sometimes, and it usually lasts just a few seconds. It feels like my face wants to move, and then it stops, and I feel better after it happens. I don’t really know what triggers it, but my dad said he notices it more in the late afternoon sometimes. Doctor: Has the patient experienced any other symptoms such as fatigue, stress, changes in vision, or any other unusual movements besides the eye twitch? Patient: No, I don’t feel tired or stressed, and I don’t have any other unusual movements besides the eye twitch. I just notice my face sometimes moving on its own, but it doesn’t hurt, and I can keep doing whatever I’m doing, like playing soccer or eating. Dad said he didn’t see anything else besides the twitch. Doctor: Has the patient experienced any other symptoms such as headaches, visual changes, or difficulty with coordination? Have there been any recent illnesses or changes in routine that might be relevant? Patient: No, I don’t have headaches or any visual changes, and I don’t have trouble with coordination. I’ve been eating

Patient: I'm three years old, and I'm a girl. I came in because I've been having this twitch in my right eye, and my dad noticed it a couple of weeks ago. He brought me to see you because he was worried about it.
Doctor: Could you please provide your full name and any relevant family medical history?
Patient: My name is Karen Nelson. I don't really know about family medical history, but my dad said there's no history of seizures in our family, and he didn't hear of anything like Tourette's before.
Doctor: Can you describe the nature of the twitch in your right eye? For example, how often does it happen, how long does each twitch last, and is there anything that seems to trigger it?
Patient: The twitch happens a few times an hour sometimes, and it usually lasts just a few seconds. It feels like my face wants to move, and then it stops, and I feel better after it happens. I don’t really know what triggers it, but my dad said he notices it more in the late afternoon sometimes.
Doctor: Has the patient experienced any other symptoms such as fatigue, stress, changes in vision, or any other unusual movements besides the eye twitch?
Patient: No, I don’t feel tired or stressed, and I don’t have any other unusual movements besides the eye twitch. Dad said he didn’t see anything else besides the twitch.
Doctor: Has the patient experienced any other symptoms such as headaches, visual changes, or difficulty with coordination? Have there been any recent illnesses or changes in routine that might be relevant?
Patient: No, I don’t have headaches or any visual changes, and I don’t have trouble with coordination. I’ve been eating well, playing with my friends, and going to soccer every Saturday. I don’t think anything else has changed recently except for the twitch.
Doctor: Have you or any close family members been diagnosed with conditions such as epilepsy, Tourette's syndrome, or other movement disorders?
Patient: No, I don’t think anyone in my family has been diagnosed with epilepsy or Tourette's or anything like that. subjective.unit: Chief Complaint: Painful, red, and warm big toe, especially with movement or pressure.
subjective.citation_text: Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today? Patient: I'm 45 years old and male. I came in because my big toe has been hurting a lot, especially when I walk or move it, and it's also red and warm to the touch. It's been bothering me for about two weeks, and it's really affecting my ability to do things like walk around or even stand for long periods. Doctor: Have you experienced similar symptoms in the past, and if so, how were they treated? Also, do you have a history of gout, arthritis, diabetes, or any other relevant medical conditions? Patient: I don't think I've ever had anything like this before. I don't have any history of gout, arthritis, diabetes, or anything like that. I was just fine until this started happening a couple of weeks ago. Doctor: Have you noticed any swelling or drainage from the affected big toe? Patient: No, I haven't noticed any swelling or drainage from my big toe. It's just red, warm, and really painful, especially when I move it or put pressure on it. It's been getting worse over the past couple of weeks. Doctor: Could you please provide information about your family history, specifically if any of your close relatives have had gout, arthritis, or similar conditions? Patient: I don't have any information about my family history, so I can't say for sure. But as far as I know, none of my close relatives have had gout, arthritis, or anything similar to what I'm experiencing. Doctor: Have you experienced any recent trauma or injury to the affected toe? Patient: No, I don't remember any injury to my toe. I just started having the pain a couple of weeks ago, and it got really bad last week when I was at that trade show. I couldn't walk much, and it hurt all the time. I didn't think it was anything

subjective.unit: Chief Complaint: Asthma symptoms during sports, feeling down lately
subjective.citation_text: Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today? Patient: I'm 16 years old, and I'm here because I've been having trouble with my asthma, especially during sports, and I've been feeling really down lately. I was hoping we could talk about it. Doctor: Can you describe the frequency and severity of your asthma symptoms during sports, and what specific medications have you been using to manage them? Patient: Sure, so I have an albuterol inhaler, and I use it whenever I start having trouble. It usually happens during any kind of aerobic workout, like when I'm playing water polo. When it happens, I start feeling like there's phlegm in my throat, my chest gets tight, I wheeze, and I have to sit down or I get lightheaded. The inhaler helps a little, but I still have to stop and catch my breath, and sometimes I get shaky after using it. Doctor: Could you provide more details about the recent feelings of being down, such as how long you've been feeling this way, any specific triggers, and whether you've experienced any changes in sleep, appetite, or interest in activities? Patient: I think the feelings of being down started around when I began this school year. It's mostly because of the stress from my AP classes and SATs. I feel really tired a lot, and I don't really feel like doing anything anymore. My friends go out, but I just want to stay home. I haven't really noticed changes in my sleep or appetite, but I do feel like there's a lot of pressure on me. Doctor: Have you had any recent chest X-rays, pulmonary function tests, or other respiratory evaluations? Patient: No, I haven't had any recent chest X-rays or pulmonary function tests. I just use my inhaler whenever I have an attack, and I haven't been to the doctor for any other respiratory evaluations. Doctor: Have you experienced any changes in your mood or energy

Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today?
Patient: I'm 16 years old, and I'm here because I've been having trouble with my asthma, especially during sports, and I've been feeling really down lately. I was hoping we could talk about it.
Doctor: Can you describe the frequency and severity of your asthma symptoms during sports, and what specific medications have you been using to manage them?
Patient: Sure, so I have an albuterol inhaler, and I use it whenever I start having trouble. It usually happens during any kind of aerobic workout, like when I'm playing water polo. When it happens, I start feeling like there's phlegm in my throat, my chest gets tight, I wheeze, and I have to sit down or I get lightheaded. The inhaler helps a little, but I still have to stop and catch my breath, and sometimes I get shaky after using it.
Doctor: Could you provide more details about the recent feelings of being down, such as how long you've been feeling this way, any specific triggers, and whether you've experienced any changes in sleep, appetite, or interest in activities?
Patient: I think the feelings of being down started around when I began this school year. It's mostly because of the stress from my AP classes and SATs. I feel really tired a lot, and I don't really feel like doing anything anymore. My friends go out, but I just want to stay home. I haven't really noticed changes in my sleep or appetite, but I do feel like there's a lot of pressure on me.
Doctor: Have you had any recent chest X-rays, pulmonary function tests, or other respiratory evaluations?
Patient: No, I haven't had any recent chest X-rays or pulmonary function tests. I just use my inhaler whenever I have an attack, and I haven't been to the doctor for any other respiratory evaluations.
Doctor: Have you experienced any changes in your mood or energy levels that are not related to your academic stress or asthma symptoms?
Patient: No, I don't think so. Most of the time, I feel like my mood and energy levels are connected to either my asthma or the stress from school. I haven't noticed any other factors affecting how I feel.
Doctor: Have you undergone any pulmonary function tests or chest X-rays in the past? If not, would you be willing to schedule these tests to better evaluate your asthma symptoms?
Patient: No, I haven't had any pulmonary function tests or chest X-rays in the past. I just use my inhaler whenever I have an attack, and I haven't been to the doctor for any other respiratory evaluations. I'm willing to schedule these tests if it would help better understand what's going on with my asthma.
Doctor: Has the patient experienced any episodes of significant sadness, hopelessness, or loss of interest in activities they once enjoyed over the past few months?
Patient: Yes, I have felt really down a lot lately, and I don't really feel like doing anything anymore. I used to enjoy hanging out with friends and playing water polo, but now I just feel really tired and don't have the motivation to do anything. It's been pretty tough.
Doctor: Have you had any recent episodes of acute respiratory distress or been hospitalized for asthma in the past?
Patient: No, I haven't had any recent episodes of acute respiratory distress or been hospitalized for asthma. I just use my inhaler when I have an attack, and I usually manage to get through it by sitting down and breathing slowly. It's not great, but it hasn't gotten to the point where I needed to go to the hospital.
Doctor: How long has the patient been experiencing feelings of being down, and has there been any change in the frequency or intensity of these feelings over time?
Patient: The feelings of being down have been going on for a few months now, especially since I started this school year. It seems like they've gotten worse over time, especially with all the stress from school and the asthma issues making it harder to keep up with sports and social stuff. It's been pretty tough to deal with.
Doctor: Has the patient undergone any pulmonary function tests or chest X-rays in the past? If not, would they be willing to schedule these tests to better evaluate their asthma symptoms?
Patient: No, I haven't had any pulmonary function tests or chest X-rays in the past. I just use my inhaler when I have an attack, and I haven't been to the doctor for any other respiratory evaluations. I'm willing to schedule these tests if it would help better understand what's going on with my asthma.
Doctor: Can you describe the specific triggers for your asthma symptoms during sports, and have you noticed any patterns or worsening of symptoms in relation to your academic stress or social withdrawal?
Patient: Sure, during sports, especially when I'm doing something aerobic like running or playing water polo, I start to feel like there's phlegm building up in my throat, my chest gets tight, and I start wheezing. It usually happens pretty quickly, and I have to stop and sit down to catch my breath. I do notice that my symptoms seem to get worse when I'm stressed about school or when I'm feeling down, which makes it harder to keep up with sports and social stuff. It feels like everything is kind of connected.
Doctor: Has the patient experienced any recent exacerbations of asthma symptoms that required additional use of the albuterol inhaler or any other rescue medications?
Patient: No, I haven't had any recent exacerbations that required more use of my inhaler than usual. I still use it when I have an attack, usually two puffs, and it helps me feel better after a while, but I still have to sit down and catch my breath. It's been pretty consistent with how it's been happening during sports.
Doctor: Have you experienced any changes in your sleep patterns or appetite since the onset of your feelings of being down?
Patient: No, I haven't really noticed any big changes in my sleep or appetite, but I do feel more tired than usual, especially after having an asthma attack during sports. I guess I just don't have as much energy as I used to, and I'm not as motivated to do the things I used to enjoy.
Doctor: Have you undergone any pulmonary function tests or chest X-rays in the past? If not, would you be willing to schedule these tests to better evaluate your asthma?
Patient: No, I haven't had any pulmonary function tests or chest X-rays in the past. I just use my inhaler when I have an attack, and I haven't been to the doctor for any other respiratory evaluations. I'm willing to schedule these tests if it would help better understand what's going on with my asthma.
Doctor: Have you experienced any episodes of acute respiratory distress, such as severe shortness of breath, chest pain, or cyanosis, in the past?
Patient: No, I haven't had any episodes of severe shortness of breath, chest pain, or anything like that. The worst it gets is wheezing, chest tightness, and needing to sit down and catch my breath, but I don't feel like I'm in immediate danger or anything like that. It's more of a struggle during sports than something really severe.

Patient: Hi, I'm Virginia. I'm here because I hurt my knee playing basketball. I was playing with Jerry, and he ran into me, and I fell to the ground. My knee has been hurting on the inside ever since, and it's still swollen. I had ice and an ace wrap, but I can't really put weight on it.
Doctor: Can you describe the exact location of the pain on your knee and whether it radiates to other areas? Have you experienced any locking, clicking, or giving way of the knee since the injury?

Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today?
Patient: I'm 45 years old, and I'm male. I've been having trouble swallowing, especially with bigger pieces of food, and it hurts when I swallow down in my chest. It's been going on for a few weeks.
Doctor: Have you experienced any weight loss, regurgitation, or chest pain associated with your dysphagia? Have you been evaluated for GERD or other esophageal disorders in the past?
Patient: No, I haven't lost any weight—I actually gained some, which is frustrating. I haven't had any regurgitation, but the chest pain when I swallow is pretty consistent. I don't think I've ever been checked for GERD or anything like that before.
Doctor: Could you describe the nature of the chest pain you experience when swallowing? For example, is it sharp, burning, or pressure-like? Does it radiate to other areas, such as your back or arms? Also, have you noticed any changes in your appetite or difficulty with eating over the past few weeks?
Patient: The pain feels like a burning sensation in my chest, especially when I swallow bigger pieces of food. It doesn't really radiate anywhere else, just stays in that area. I haven't really noticed a change in my appetite, but I do find it harder to eat certain things because of the discomfort.
Doctor: Have you undergone any imaging or endoscopic evaluations of the esophagus or upper gastrointestinal tract?
Patient: No, I haven't had any imaging or endoscopic evaluations of my esophagus or upper gastrointestinal tract yet. The doctor mentioned something about a barium swallow, but I wasn't sure what that was exactly. I just came in because I've been having trouble swallowing and the pain has been getting me worried.
Doctor: Have you experienced any difficulty swallowing liquids or only solids? Have you noticed any changes in your voice or coughing while eating?
Patient: I haven't had any trouble swallowing liquids, just the bigger pieces of food. I don't cough while eating, and my voice hasn't changed. It's just the solid foods that feel like they get stuck and cause the burning pain in my chest.
Doctor: Have you experienced any recent weight loss, changes in bowel habits, or a family history of esophageal disorders or gastrointestinal cancers?
Patient: No, I haven't experienced any recent weight loss or changes in my bowel habits. As for family history, I don't think there's anything related to esophageal disorders or gastrointestinal cancers that I'm aware of.
Doctor: Have you ever been diagnosed with any autoimmune conditions, such as scleroderma or lupus, or have you been exposed to any caustic substances that could affect the esophagus?
Patient: No, I don't think I've ever been diagnosed with any autoimmune conditions like scleroderma or lupus, and I don't recall being exposed to anything caustic that could affect my esophagus. I've just been dealing with this swallowing issue and the chest pain for a while now.
Doctor: Have you undergone any endoscopic evaluations of the upper gastrointestinal tract, such as an upper endoscopy, in the past?
Patient: No, I haven't undergone any endoscopic evaluations of the upper gastrointestinal tract in the past. The doctor mentioned something about scheduling me for an upper endoscopy, but that's the first time I've heard of it. I just came in because I've been having trouble swallowing and the pain has been getting me worried.
Doctor: Have you noticed any changes in your ability to swallow liquids, or have you experienced any difficulty with breathing or coughing while eating?
Patient: No, I haven't noticed any changes in my ability to swallow liquids, and I don't have any difficulty breathing or coughing while eating. It's just the solid foods that feel like they get stuck and cause the burning pain in my chest.
Doctor: Have you experienced any unintentional weight loss, vomiting, or difficulty swallowing liquids in the past few months?
Patient: No, I haven't experienced any unintentional weight loss or vomiting in the past few months. I actually mentioned that I've gained some weight, which is the opposite of what I was expecting with these symptoms. I haven't had trouble swallowing liquids, just the bigger pieces of food.
Doctor: Have you had any recent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy or barium swallow studies scheduled or performed?
Patient: No, I haven't had any recent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy or barium swallow studies performed. The doctor mentioned scheduling me for an upper endoscopy, but that’s the first time I’ve heard of it. I just came in because I’ve been having trouble swallowing and the pain has been getting me worried.
Doctor: Thank you for sharing that with me. I understand your concern about the difficulty swallowing and the chest pain. To better understand your condition, could you tell me if you've noticed any changes in your ability to eat over the past few weeks? For example, have you started avoiding certain foods or noticed any weight changes?
Patient: Over the past few weeks, I've been avoiding foods that are harder to chew, like meat or bread, because they feel like they get stuck and cause pain when I swallow. I've been eating more soft foods or things that are easier to chew, like pizza or burgers, but even those sometimes bother me. I didn't lose weight, which is surprising because I thought I might, but I actually gained a little weight instead.
Doctor: Have you had any recent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy or barium swallow studies performed? If not, would you be willing to schedule an upper endoscopy to evaluate for possible esophageal pathology?
Patient: No, I haven't had any recent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy or barium swallow studies performed. The doctor mentioned scheduling me for an upper endoscopy, but that’s the first time I’ve heard of it. I’m willing to schedule it if it will help figure out what’s going on with my swallowing and the pain I’m having. I just want to get better and make sure there’s nothing serious.
Doctor: Have you experienced any difficulty with swallowing liquids as well, or is it only solids? Additionally, have you noticed any changes in your voice or coughing while eating?
Patient: No, I haven't had any difficulty swallowing liquids, just the bigger pieces of food. I haven't noticed any changes in my voice or coughing while eating either. It's mostly the solid foods that feel like they get stuck and cause the burning pain in my chest.
Doctor: Have you experienced any episodes of chest pain unrelated to swallowing, such as during physical exertion or at rest, which could suggest a cardiac cause?
Patient: No, I haven't had any chest pain unrelated to swallowing. The pain is specifically when I swallow, especially with bigger pieces of food. It feels like a burning sensation in my chest, but it doesn't happen when I'm exerting myself or at rest.

Patient: I'm 46 years old, and I'm here because I've been having a lot of trouble sleeping. I feel like I'm choking and can't catch my breath a few minutes after I lay down. It's been going on for about two weeks.
Doctor: Have you experienced any other symptoms such as loud snoring, gasping for air during sleep, or excessive daytime sleepiness? Have you been evaluated for any heart disease or respiratory conditions in the past?
Patient: I don't snore, and I don't remember gasping for air, but I do feel really tired during the day. I have a history of back pain, diabetes, and they mentioned I have CHF and COPD, but I don't remember being evaluated for heart disease specifically.
Doctor: Could you please describe the frequency and severity of the choking sensation and shortness of breath when lying down? Have you noticed any chest pain or palpitations during these episodes? * **Treatment Plan, Medications, and Follow-up:** The patient will continue to rest, elevate, and ice his left ankle. He will also take ibuprofen as needed for pain relief. subjective.unit: Chief Complaint: Painful left ankle injury
subjective.citation_text: Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today? Patient: Hey, I'm Matthew. I'm 35, male. I hurt my left ankle when I stepped off the curb wrong while walking with my wife yesterday. It's been really painful, and I wanted to get checked out. Doctor: Could you please confirm your age, gender, and describe the injury to your left ankle in more detail, including when it occurred and what you were doing at the time? Patient: Sure, I was on a walk with my wife yesterday when I stepped off the curb and landed on my left ankle wrong. It happened pretty suddenly, and it's been really painful ever since, especially on the outside of my ankle. I didn't hear a pop, but it felt like it stretched a lot, and it's been killing me for a couple of days now. Doctor: Have you experienced any swelling, bruising, or difficulty bearing weight on your left ankle since the injury? Patient: Yes, there's some swelling and bruising on the outside of my ankle, and it's been really hard to put weight on it. I was able to walk back home, but it was very painful. I've been elevating it, icing it, and taking ibuprofen to help with the pain. Doctor: Have you experienced any prior ankle injuries, surgeries, or chronic conditions that might affect the current injury? Patient: No, I don't think I've had any substantial injuries to that ankle before. Nothing that I would say was significant in the past. Doctor: Have you noticed any deformity or instability in the left ankle since the injury? Have you experienced any numbness, tingling, or weakness in the foot or toes? Patient: No, I haven't noticed any deformity or instability in my left ankle, and I don't have any numbness, tingling, or weakness in my foot or toes. Everything feels normal in terms of sensation and movement, other than the pain and swelling. Doctor: Have you had any

Patient: The pain has been pretty consistent, maybe a little less sharp today, but it's still been really bothering me. The swelling hasn't gone down much either. It's been pretty steady since the injury.
