Patient: I have been taking some ibuprofen and trying to elevate and ice it, and keep my weight off of it. It's helped a little, maybe bringing the pain down to a seven when I take the medication, but it's still pretty uncomfortable. I haven't done any specific rehabilitation exercises yet.
Doctor: Have you noticed any numbness, tingling, or weakness in your foot or toes since the injury?

subjective.citation_text: Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today? Patient: Hi, I'm Anna. I'm not sure about my exact age, but I'm in my late twenties. I came in because I hurt my right ankle after falling on some ice last night. It popped when I fell, and it's been hurting a lot, though I can put a little weight on it now. Doctor: Have you experienced any previous injuries or conditions affecting your right ankle? Patient: No, I don't think I've ever injured this particular ankle before. I used to play soccer in high school and had other injuries, but nothing like this. I knew it was time to come in because I couldn't walk on it at first and it's still pretty sore. Doctor: Could you describe the exact location of the pain in your right ankle and rate it on a scale from 1 to 10? Also, have you noticed any swelling, bruising, or deformity since the injury? Patient: The pain is on the outside of my ankle, near the bone, and it's a throbbing pain that's constant. I'd say it's around a 6 now, though it was worse right after the fall. There's some bruising and swelling, especially on the lateral side, and it feels a little warm to the touch. Doctor: Have you noticed any deformity, instability, or difficulty moving your ankle? Are there any neurological symptoms such as numbness, tingling, or weakness in your foot or ankle? Patient: No, I haven't noticed any deformity or instability, but it does feel a bit wobbly when I try to move it. And I don't have any numbness, tingling, or weakness in my foot or ankle. My friend had to help me get inside after I fell, and I'm still limping a bit, but I can put some weight on it now. Doctor: Have you had any imaging studies or X-rays of your ankle since the injury? Patient: Yes,

subjective.unit: Chief Complaint: Fatigue, lightheadedness, and bloating.
subjective.citation_text: Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today? Patient: I'm 58 years old, male. I've been feeling out of sorts lately—just tired, fatigued, and sometimes lightheaded. I also feel bloated now and then. I wanted to come in for a check-up because I've been struggling with some of my usual symptoms again. Doctor: Could you please confirm your age, gender, and the specific symptoms you're experiencing, including how long you've been feeling fatigued, lightheaded, or bloated? Patient: I'm 58 years old, male. The fatigue and lightheadedness have been going on for about five weeks now, since around Labor Day. I've also been feeling bloated every once in a while, and it's been a bit harder to keep up with my diet lately because of some home renovations we've been doing. Doctor: Have you experienced any chest pain, shortness of breath, or palpitations during the episodes of fatigue or lightheadedness? Have you had any prior cardiovascular evaluations, such as an ECG or echocardiogram? Patient: I've had some slight chest cramps, but they usually go away after an hour or so. I don't really feel like I'm having palpitations, but I do get short of breath sometimes when I'm exerting myself, like when I'm working on the home projects. I've had some tests done before, like an echocardiogram, which I think showed that my heart's pumping function is a little reduced. Doctor: Could you please share the specific ejection fraction value from your previous echocardiogram? Also, have you experienced any other symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, or changes in bowel habits that might be related to your bloating? Patient: I don't remember the exact number, but I was told that the pumping function of my heart is a little reduced. As for other symptoms, I haven't had nausea, vomiting, or changes in my bowel habits—just the bloating now and then. Doctor: Could you please provide

Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today?
Patient: I'm 62 years old, and I'm here for my annual exam. I've been managing my depression and hypertension, and I had a lobectomy a few years back. It's been a while since my last checkup, so I wanted to come in for an update.
Doctor: Could you please provide your age, gender, and the reason for your visit today?
Patient: I'm 62 years old, male, and I'm here for my annual exam. I've been managing my depression and hypertension, and I had a lobectomy a few years back. It's been a while since my last checkup, so I wanted to come in for an update.
Doctor: Could you please tell me if you have any current symptoms or concerns you'd like to discuss during this visit?
Patient: I've been feeling relatively okay overall, but I did have a tough spring with all the pollen and allergies. It was also a stressful time with my daughter moving out for college. I've been managing my depression pretty well with my medication, but my hypertension has been a bit more of a struggle, especially on the weekends when I sometimes forget to take my meds. I also run 4 to 5 miles a day, and sometimes when it's humid, I feel a little short of breath and get a bit of a pounding in my chest, but it usually goes away.
Doctor: Have you experienced any episodes of chest pain, dizziness, or syncope during or after your runs, especially in humid conditions?
Patient: No, I haven't had any chest pain, dizziness, or fainting during or after my runs. The pounding in my chest usually goes away on its own, and I don't feel lightheaded or anything like that. It's more of a mild sensation, and I don't worry about it too much.
Doctor: Could you provide details about your family history of cardiovascular disease, including any history of heart attacks, strokes, or hypertension in first-degree relatives?
Patient: I don't have specific information about my family history of cardiovascular disease. I know I have a history of hypertension, but I'm not sure about my relatives' medical histories. I don't think it's been discussed much with me before.
Doctor: Could you provide more details about your family history of cardiovascular disease, including any known conditions such as hypertension, coronary artery disease, or heart failure in first-degree relatives?
Patient: I don't have specific information about my family history of cardiovascular disease. I know I have a history of hypertension, but I'm not sure about my relatives' medical histories. I don't think it's been discussed much with me before.
Doctor: Could you provide more details about the duration and frequency of your shortness of breath and chest pounding during physical activity? Additionally, have you noticed any specific triggers or patterns associated with these symptoms?
Patient: The shortness of breath and chest pounding usually happen when it's humid, especially during my morning runs. It doesn't happen every time, but when it does, it's more noticeable. It usually goes away on its own after a few minutes, and I don't really have any specific triggers other than the weather and exertion.
Doctor: Has the patient experienced any episodes of syncope, palpitations, or chest pain during or after physical activity? If so, please describe the nature, duration, and any associated symptoms.
Patient: No, I haven't experienced any episodes of syncope, palpitations, or chest pain during or after physical activity. The pounding in my chest is mild and usually goes away on its own after a few minutes. I don't feel lightheaded or have any other symptoms with it.
Doctor: Could you describe the exact nature of the chest pounding you feel? Does it feel like a rapid heartbeat, a fluttering sensation, or something else? Also, have you noticed any patterns in when these episodes occur, such as specific times of day or types of activity?
Patient: The chest pounding feels like a slight, rhythmic thumping in my chest, almost like my heart is beating a little harder than usual. It doesn't feel like a flutter or anything crazy—it's more of a mild sensation. It usually happens when I'm running, especially on humid days, but it doesn't happen every time. I don't really notice it at other times of the day or with other activities.
Doctor: Could you describe if you've had any recent episodes of dizziness, faintness, or palpitations during or after these episodes? If so, how long do they last, and are they associated with any specific activities or triggers?
Patient: No, I haven't had any recent episodes of dizziness, faintness, or palpitations during or after those moments. The chest pounding is mild and goes away on its own after a few minutes. I don't feel lightheaded or have any other symptoms with it.
Doctor: How long does each episode of chest pounding typically last, and how frequently do these episodes occur during physical activity?
Patient: Each episode of chest pounding usually lasts a few minutes, maybe up to five or so, and it doesn't happen every time I run. It's more like once in a while, especially on the hotter, more humid days.
Doctor: Has the patient experienced any episodes of chest pain, dizziness, or syncope during or after the chest pounding episodes? If so, please describe the nature, duration, and any associated symptoms.
Patient: No, I haven't experienced any chest pain, dizziness, or syncope during or after the chest pounding episodes. The pounding is mild and goes away on its own after a few minutes. I don't feel lightheaded or have any other symptoms with it.
Doctor: Have you noticed any changes in the frequency or intensity of the chest pounding episodes over the past few months? Are there any specific activities or times of day when the episodes are more likely to occur?
Patient: No, I haven't noticed any changes in the frequency or intensity of the chest pounding over the past few months. It still happens occasionally, mostly when I'm running on hot or humid days, but it doesn't happen every time. I don't really notice it at other times of day or with other activities.
Doctor: Have you had any recent changes in your medication regimen for hypertension or depression, or any new medications started recently?
Patient: No, I haven't had any recent changes in my medication regimen for hypertension or depression, and I haven't started any new medications recently. I've been staying on the same medications as before, and they've been working pretty well for me.
Doctor: Have you had any episodes of palpitations, lightheadedness, or syncope in the past, even if not related to the current symptoms?
Patient: No, I don't recall having any episodes of palpitations, lightheadedness, or syncope in the past, even ones not related to the current symptoms. I've been pretty stable overall, and the only thing I've noticed recently is that mild chest pounding during runs on hot days, which goes away on its own.

subjective.unit: Chief Complaint: Iron deficiency anemia
subjective.citation_text: Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today? Patient: I'm 65 years old, and I'm a female. I've been dealing with iron deficiency anemia for a long time, and I came in because I was told I was anemic again when I tried to donate blood in December. I've been feeling really tired, having chills, and even some wheezing when I try to be active. It's been frustrating not knowing why this keeps happening. Doctor: Could you provide more details about your dietary habits, including any changes in your intake of iron-rich foods or supplements, and whether you have a history of menstrual bleeding or gastrointestinal issues that might contribute to iron deficiency? Patient: I don't have a history of menstrual bleeding anymore since I had a hysterectomy in 1996. As for my diet, I haven't really made any changes to eat more iron-rich foods, but I did start taking iron pills again about a year ago after not taking them for some time. I also take over-the-counter vitamin B12 supplements. I don't have any known gastrointestinal issues, but I do get cold easily and have been feeling more anxious and depressed lately. Doctor: Could you provide details about any recent gastrointestinal symptoms, such as changes in bowel habits, abdominal pain, or black stools? Additionally, have you undergone any upper or lower gastrointestinal endoscopy or imaging studies to evaluate for potential sources of blood loss? Patient: I don't have any changes in my bowel habits or abdominal pain, and I haven't noticed any black stools. I had a colonoscopy about five to six years ago, and it was normal with no polyps. They said to come back in 10 years, so I haven't had an upper endoscopy yet. Doctor: Have you had any recent upper endoscopy or capsule endoscopy to evaluate for potential sources of chronic gastrointestinal blood loss, such as angiodysplasia or small bowel lesions? Patient: No, I haven't had an upper endoscopy or capsule endoscopy yet. The doctor mentioned

I slipped while doing my laundry, tried to catch myself, and my wrist started hurting really badly and got swollen. It's been like that since yesterday morning, and it's still really painful, especially when I try to move it. Doctor: Could you please provide your age and gender, and describe the injury in more detail, such as how it occurred and whether you heard a popping sound or felt any deformity at the time? Patient: I'm sorry, I didn't mention my age earlier. I'm 32, and I'm female. As for the injury, I slipped on the stairs while doing my laundry, tried to catch myself, and my wrist started hurting really badly. I didn't hear a popping sound, but it got really swollen and it's been like that since yesterday morning. It's just really bad when I try to move it. Doctor: Have you experienced any prior wrist injuries, fractures, or surgeries? Do you have a history of any medical conditions such as diabetes, osteoporosis, or rheumatoid arthritis? Are you currently taking any medications or supplements? Patient: No, I haven't injured this arm before, and I don't have any of those medical conditions. I'm not on any medications or supplements right now, just took some ibuprofen for the pain. Doctor: Could you describe the mechanism of the fall in more detail, such as how you slipped and whether your hand was in a specific position when you landed? Patient: I was walking up and down the stairs doing my laundry, and I slipped. I tried to catch myself by putting my arms out, but I missed a step and fell, which is when my wrist started hurting really badly. My hand was kind of bent when I landed, and that’s when the pain and swelling started. Doctor: Have you noticed any deformity or abnormal positioning

Doctor: Could you please provide details about the timeline of your diagnosis, including when the biopsy was performed and when the neoadjuvant chemotherapy started and ended?
Patient: I was diagnosed with stage three non-small cell lung cancer, and the biopsy was done before starting the neoadjuvant chemotherapy. I had my last treatment just a few days ago, and I'm here for a follow-up to see how I'm doing.
Doctor: Could you please provide details about the timeline of your diagnosis, the biopsy procedure, and the specific regimen and duration of your neoadjuvant chemotherapy? Additionally, have you experienced any symptoms or side effects since completing your last treatment?
Patient: I had my last treatment just a few days ago, and I’ve been tolerating it pretty well. I have a minimal cough and a sore throat, and I’ve been feeling a little more tired than usual, but I haven’t had any nausea or vomiting. I haven’t noticed any shortness of breath, just a dry cough that comes and goes.
Doctor: Could you please provide details about the specific neoadjuvant chemotherapy regimen you received, including the drugs used, dosages, and the duration of treatment?
Patient: I was on a combination of two chemotherapies, cisplatin and etoposide. I don't know the exact dosages, but I was getting it for a while before my last treatment just a few days ago. I’ve been tolerating it pretty well overall.
Doctor: Could you please describe the duration and severity of your cough and sore throat? Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight since starting the chemotherapy? Additionally, could you tell me how your fatigue is affecting your daily activities?

I haven’t had much of an appetite lately, so I’m not eating as much as I normally would, but I haven’t lost weight yet. The fatigue is there, but it’s not overwhelming; it just makes me feel a little more tired than usual, but I can still manage my daily activities.

Doctor: Have you traveled to any areas known for high tick activity in the past month, and have you been exposed to any other potential sources of infection? Patient: I've been out in the woods and spending a lot of time in my yard, which is probably where I got the tick bite. Doctor: Have you experienced any neurological symptoms such as tingling, numbness

subjective.unit: Chief Complaint: Arm hurting near the wrist.
subjective.citation_text: Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today? Patient: Hello. I'm 43 years old, female. I came in because my arm has been hurting near my wrist. It started after I hit the pole of the net while playing tennis, and it jarred my arm. It's been swollen a little and hurts when I move my wrist. Doctor: Have you experienced any numbness, tingling, or weakness in your hand or fingers? Have you had any prior injuries or conditions affecting your wrist or arm? Patient: No numbness in my hand, but there's a little pain when I move my wrist. As for prior injuries, I had a trauma from falling on a rake while doing lawn work. I don’t remember any other issues with my wrist or arm before this. Doctor: Could you describe the specific movements that cause pain, the presence of any clicking or locking in the wrist, and whether you have experienced any weakness or difficulty gripping objects? Patient: The movements that cause pain are when I bend my wrist or flex my thumb. I don’t feel any clicking or locking in my wrist, and I haven’t had any trouble gripping objects, but it does hurt when I move it a certain way. Doctor: Could you please describe the location of the swelling and whether there is any bruising or deformity visible on your wrist? Patient: The swelling is on the part of my arm near my wrist, and there's no bruising or deformity that I can see. It's just a little puffy, nothing too bad. Doctor: Could you please describe the specific location of the tenderness on your wrist and whether there is any associated stiffness or difficulty in performing daily activities? Patient: The tenderness is on the part of my arm near my wrist, right around where I hit it on the pole. It's pretty sore when they press there, and it's stiff sometimes, especially when I try to move my wrist or flex my thumb. It makes some daily activities a bit harder, like opening jars or typing

Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today?
Patient: Hello. I'm a 42-year-old female. I hurt my finger while I was skiing this past weekend. I jammed my index finger on something, but I'm not sure what. It's been hurting for about five days now.
Doctor: Could you please provide your age, gender, and a detailed description of your current symptoms, including when they started and any associated pain or swelling?
Patient: I'm 42 years old, and I'm a female. I hurt my right index finger while I was skiing on Saturday. It's been about five days since the injury, and it's been hurting pretty badly—like a seven out of 10. It doesn't really swell, but it definitely aches, and it hurts when I move it or touch it.
Doctor: Could you please describe the exact location of the pain on your finger, and have you noticed any changes in its appearance, such as bruising, discoloration, or difficulty moving it?
Patient: The pain is on my right index finger, specifically near the tip, and it hurts when I move it or touch it. I don’t think it’s bruised or discolored, but it’s pretty sore. It’s hard to bend it fully without pain.
Doctor: Have you noticed any deformity, numbness, tingling, or weakness in your right index finger since the injury?
Patient: No, I haven't noticed any deformity, numbness, tingling, or weakness in my right index finger since the injury. It's just sore and painful when I move it or touch it.
Doctor: Have you had any prior fractures or injuries to your right index finger?
Patient: No, I don't think I've had any prior fractures or injuries to my right index finger. This is the first time it's ever hurt like this.
Doctor: Have you undergone any imaging or medical evaluation for this injury, such as X-rays or a visit to a healthcare provider?
Patient: No, I haven't had any imaging or medical evaluation for this injury yet. I just started taking some ibuprofen, but it didn't really help with the pain. I haven't seen a healthcare provider for it before today.
Doctor: Have you noticed any deformity in your right index finger, such as it appearing bent or out of place? Also, can you move the finger fully without pain, or is there any stiffness or limitation in movement?
Patient: No, I haven't noticed any deformity in my right index finger—it doesn't look bent or out of place. I can move it, but it's pretty stiff and painful, especially when I try to bend it fully. It's hard to use it normally without discomfort.
Doctor: Have you undergone any physical examination of the right index finger by a healthcare provider, and if so, what were the findings?
Patient: No, I haven't undergone any physical examination of my right index finger by a healthcare provider before today. I just came in because of the pain and stiffness, and the doctor is examining it now. I don't know what the findings will be yet.
Doctor: Can you describe the nature of the pain in your right index finger? Is it sharp, dull, throbbing, or burning? Also, have you ever had any history of autoimmune or inflammatory conditions, such as rheumatoid arthritis or lupus?
Patient: The pain is more of a sharp, aching feeling, especially when I move the finger or touch it. It's not burning or throbbing, just sore and uncomfortable. As for autoimmune or inflammatory conditions, I don't think I have any of those. I don't have a history of rheumatoid arthritis or lupus.
Doctor: Has the patient undergone any imaging studies, such as X-rays or MRI, for the right index finger injury?
Patient: No, I haven't had any imaging studies for the injury yet. The doctor just showed me the X-ray here, and it looked normal, but I wasn't sure what to expect before that.
Doctor: Could you describe the exact location of the tenderness on your finger and whether there is any specific movement or activity that makes the pain worse?
Patient: The tenderness is right at the tip of my index finger, near where it bends. It hurts the most when I try to bend it or when someone touches it. It also hurts when I try to grip things or make a fist.
Doctor: Have you experienced any recent repetitive strain or overuse of the right index finger prior to the skiing injury?
Patient: No, I don't think I've done anything repetitive with my finger before the skiing accident. It was just the sudden injury when I flipped while skiing that caused the pain and stiffness. I haven't been using it a lot since then because it hurts too much.
Doctor: Have you noticed any stiffness or difficulty moving the finger beyond just bending it, and does the pain worsen with specific movements or activities?
Patient: The stiffness is mainly when I try to bend the finger, and it's hard to make a fist or grip things. The pain gets worse when I move it or touch it, especially when someone presses on it or when I try to flex it. It doesn't really hurt when it's just sitting still, though.
Doctor: Have you experienced any previous injuries or conditions affecting the right index finger or hand, such as sprains, strains, or tendonitis?
Patient: No, I don't think I've had any previous injuries or conditions affecting my right index finger or hand. This seems to be the first time I've had an issue with it. I don't recall any past sprains, strains, or tendonitis in that finger specifically.
Doctor: Have you experienced any previous episodes of joint pain, stiffness, or swelling in other fingers or joints, which could suggest an underlying rheumatological condition?
Patient: No, I don't think I've had any joint pain, stiffness, or swelling in other fingers or joints before. This is the first time I've had any issues like this, and it's been pretty isolated to my right index finger since the skiing accident. I don't have any other symptoms like that in my hands or elsewhere.

Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today?
Patient: Hello, Doctor. I'm 44 years old, and I'm here because I've been having a lot of pain in my left shoulder for about a week. It started after I was in a gymnastics class and I think I might have fallen into a weird position during a move. It hurts when I try to move it at all.
Doctor: Could you please confirm your age, gender, and provide more details about the shoulder pain, such as its location, intensity, and any associated symptoms?
Patient: I'm 44 years old, and I'm a female. The pain is in my left shoulder, and it hurts a lot. It started after I was in a gymnastics class, and I think I might have fallen into a weird position during a move. Any movement of my left shoulder hurts, and I haven't taken any pain medication except for Tylenol for a couple of days, but that didn't help.
Doctor: Have you noticed any swelling, bruising, or numbness/tingling in your left arm or hand since the injury?
Patient: No, I haven't noticed any swelling, bruising, or numbness or tingling in my left arm or hand since the injury. The pain is just in my shoulder, and it hurts when I move it at all.
Doctor: Have you experienced any clicking, locking, or weakness in your left shoulder since the injury? Additionally, does the pain radiate to your arm or neck?
Patient: No, I haven't experienced any clicking, locking, or weakness in my left shoulder since the injury. The pain doesn't radiate to my arm or neck—it's just in my shoulder and hurts when I move it at all.
Doctor: Could you describe the specific movement or position during the gymnastics class that caused the fall? Additionally, have you noticed any weakness, clicking, or locking in your left shoulder since the injury?
Patient: I was doing a move where I think I toppled over into some weird position, maybe went overboard, and that's when the pain started. No, I haven't noticed any weakness, clicking, or locking in my left shoulder since then. It just hurts when I try to move it at all.

Patient: No, I haven't experienced any numbness, tingling, or weakness in my left arm or hand since the injury. The pain is just in my shoulder and hurts when I move it at all.
Doctor: Could you please describe the specific movement or position during the gymnastics class that caused the pain? Additionally, have you noticed any limitation in your ability to lift your arm or perform daily activities with your left hand?
Patient: I was doing a move where I think I toppled over into some weird position, maybe went overboard, and that's when the pain started. And yeah, I have a hard time lifting my arm or doing anything with my left hand because it hurts too much.

Doctor: Could you share your current blood pressure readings and how frequently you monitor it? Additionally, have there been any recent changes in your hypertension management or treatment plan? Patient: I've been using the blood pressure cuff once a day, and my readings have been pretty normal. There haven't been any changes in my hypertension management or treatment plan recently. I'm still on the lisinopril that was prescribed. Doctor: Thank

subjective.citation_text: Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today? Patient: I'm 66 years old, and I'm a male. I've been having constant pain in my left shoulder and left elbow for about five months now. It's been pretty bad at times, and it's been really frustrating because I used to go to the gym regularly, but I haven't been able to lift much weight anymore. Doctor: Can you describe the nature of the pain in your left shoulder and elbow? For example, is it sharp, dull, or throbbing? Are there any associated symptoms such as swelling, redness, numbness, or tingling? Does the pain radiate to other areas? Patient: The pain is more of a constant ache, but it can get sharper sometimes, especially when I move my arm certain ways. It doesn't feel like it's swelling or red, and there's no tingling or numbness. It's mostly in the shoulder and elbow, and it doesn't really go anywhere else. It's just been really persistent. Doctor: Have you experienced any prior trauma, repetitive strain, or injuries to your left shoulder or elbow? Patient: Yes, I fell five months ago while walking up some icy stairs. I stepped wrong, my feet slipped, and I fell on my left side. It seemed like my shoulder and wrist took the brunt of the fall. The pain has been there ever since. Doctor: Have you undergone any imaging studies or consultations with a specialist for this condition? Patient: No, I haven't had any imaging studies or consultations with a specialist yet. I've been trying to manage it with some ice and rest, but it's still been pretty painful and limiting for me. That's why I'm here today. Doctor: Could you describe the specific movements or activities that make the pain worse, and have you noticed any weakness or limited range of motion in your left arm? Patient: The pain gets worse when I try to lift things, especially weights

Doctor: Can you describe the type of acne you have, such as blackheads, whiteheads, pimples, or cysts? Patient: I have a lot of blackheads and whiteheads, especially on my forehead, and some red bumps on my cheeks and chin. It's not too bad on my chest or back. Patient: There's no family history of acne or related skin conditions that I know of. Patient: I have a lot of blackheads and whiteheads, especially on my forehead, and some red bumps on my cheeks and chin. It's not too bad on my chest or back.

Patient: The red bumps on my cheeks and chin are kind of small and not too bad, but they’re there. I haven’t had any scarring or pain from it. I’ve been using Persa-Gel and washing my face regularly, and it’s helped a little, but not as much as I’d like.

I'm here because I've been having blood in my urine and some pain, and I had a renal ultrasound to check for kidney stones. Doctor: Could you please describe the duration and characteristics of the hematuria, such as whether it is gross or microscopic, and whether it is intermittent or persistent? Also, could you describe the nature and location of the pain, and whether it is associated with any other symptoms like fever, nausea, or vomiting? Patient: The blood in my urine has been going on for about six weeks. It’s bright red, like cherry Kool-Aid, and it’s been intermittent. I had a few episodes of really bad pain last week, like an 8 out of 10, in my lower back area. It was constant and hurt something terrible, but now it’s better after passing the stones. I didn’t have any fever, nausea, or vomiting with it. Doctor: Could you please provide the results of the renal ultrasound that was performed? Patient: The ultrasound showed that my right kidney is 10 cm long and 5 cm wide, and there were no stones, masses, or hydronephrosis. My left kidney is a bit bigger, 10.8 cm long, and there's a 6 mm stone, but it's not blocking anything. I also had a urine test today, and there was a trace amount of blood, but nothing else was abnormal. Doctor: Thank you for providing the ultrasound results. Have you experienced any other symptoms, such as frequent urination, urgency, or difficulty passing urine? Patient: Yes, I have had frequent urination and a lot of urgency, especially before I passed the stones last week. It was really uncomfortable and made me go to the bathroom constantly. Doctor: Have you experienced any dysuria, nocturia, or a history of urinary tract infections? Patient: I don't remember having any

subjective.citation_text: Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today? Patient: I'm 58 years old, and I'm here because I've been having trouble breathing more than usual. It's not something I've had before, and it's been happening in different situations, like when I'm outside or even when I'm at home. I just want to figure out what's going on. Doctor: Could you describe the duration of your shortness of breath, any associated symptoms such as chest pain, cough, or fatigue, and whether there are any specific triggers or times of day when it worsens? Patient: The shortness of breath has been happening for a while now, maybe a few months. It doesn't really have a specific time or trigger, but I notice it more when I'm outside or even at home sometimes. I don't have chest pain or a cough, but I do get tired more easily when it happens. It's kind of frustrating because I feel like I should be able to breathe easier, you know? Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today?
Patient: I'm 58 years old, and I'm here because I've been having trouble breathing more than usual. It's not something I've had before, and it's been happening in different situations, like when I'm outside or even when I'm at home. I just want to figure out what's going on.
Doctor: Could you describe the duration of your shortness of breath, any associated symptoms such as chest pain, cough, or fatigue, and whether there are any specific triggers or times of day when it worsens?
Patient: The shortness of breath has been happening for a while now, maybe a few months. It doesn't really have a specific time or trigger, but I notice it more when I'm outside or even at home sometimes. I don't have chest pain or a cough, but I do get tired more easily when it happens. It's kind of frustrating because I feel like I should be able to breathe easier, you know?
Doctor: Have you had any prior evaluations or diagnostic tests for this dyspnea, such as chest X-rays, pulmonary function tests, or blood work?
Patient: Yes, I had a chest X-ray and a pulmonary function test when I came in, and they were both normal. The doctor didn't find anything wrong with my lungs on the tests, but I still feel like I'm having trouble breathing, especially when I'm outside or at home. It's kind of confusing because the tests didn't show anything, but the symptoms are real.
Doctor: Could you describe any recent changes in your activity level or any new medications you might be taking? Additionally, have you noticed any swelling in your legs or feet?
Patient: I haven't started any new medications, but I do have an inhaler that I use when the symptoms come on. I wasn't really active before, but I try to walk around the property sometimes. I don't notice any swelling in my legs or feet, though.
Doctor: Could you please describe your physical examination findings, including your vital signs, heart sounds, and any signs of fluid retention or respiratory distress?
Patient: My vital signs look good, my pulse is okay, and my pulse ox is normal. I don't appear to be in any distress, though I might be a little nervous. My lungs exam showed some faint expiratory wheezing bilaterally, but I don't have any rash, swelling, or other issues. I was told my chest X-ray and pulmonary function test were normal.
Doctor: Have you experienced any episodes of dizziness, lightheadedness, or syncope, especially upon standing or during physical exertion?
Patient: No, I haven't had any dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting spells. I feel pretty steady on my feet, even when I'm walking around the property or doing things outside. I don't notice any issues with my balance or feeling weak when I stand up.
Doctor: Have you experienced any episodes of nocturnal dyspnea or orthopnea? Have you noticed any improvement in symptoms with the use of your inhaler?
Patient: No, I haven't had any trouble breathing at night or when lying down. The inhaler helps a little when I feel the symptoms coming on, but it doesn't completely take them away. I still feel like I'm working harder to breathe, especially when I'm outside or even at home sometimes.
Doctor: Have you experienced any palpitations, chest discomfort, or syncope in the past? Additionally, have you been evaluated for cardiac conditions such as heart failure, arrhythmias, or valvular disease?
Patient: No, I haven't had any palpitations or chest discomfort, and I haven't fainted or passed out. I don't think I've been evaluated for heart problems, but I don't feel like my heart is racing or anything like that. I just feel like my breathing is off, not my heart.
Doctor: Can you describe the exact nature of the wheezing? Is it high-pitched, low-pitched, or does it vary? Also, have you noticed any specific triggers that seem to worsen the dyspnea or wheezing?
Patient: The wheezing is more like a high-pitched sound, especially when I'm breathing out. It doesn't seem to be tied to one specific trigger, but I do notice it more when I'm outside or even sometimes when I'm at home, even when the cat isn't around. I'm not exactly sure why it happens, but it's been getting more frequent lately.
Doctor: Have you been evaluated for any cardiac conditions, such as heart failure or arrhythmias, or have you undergone any cardiac testing, such as an echocardiogram or ECG?
Patient: No, I don't think I've been evaluated for heart problems or had any tests like an echocardiogram or ECG. I just came in because of the breathing issues, and the doctor said my chest X-ray and pulmonary function test were normal. I haven't had any symptoms that make me think it's my heart.
Doctor: Have you experienced any episodes of chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath that occur with exertion or when lying flat? These could help assess for potential cardiac involvement.
Patient: No, I haven't had any chest pain or palpitations, and my shortness of breath doesn't really happen with exertion or when lying flat. It just comes on randomly, sometimes when I'm outside, sometimes when I'm at home, even when I'm not doing anything. It's more like my breathing just feels off for no real reason.
Doctor: Have you experienced any recent changes in your environment, such as exposure to new allergens, pollutants, or changes in weather patterns that might be associated with the increased frequency of your symptoms?
Patient: No, I haven't really noticed any changes in my environment that seem to be causing this. I live in the same place, and I don't think I've been exposed to anything new. It just feels like my breathing has been off more often lately, even when I'm not doing anything different. I'm not sure why it's happening more.
Doctor: Has the patient undergone any recent blood tests, such as a complete blood count (CBC), comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), or thyroid function tests?
Patient: No, I don't think I've had any blood tests recently. The doctor did mention my chest X-ray and pulmonary function test were normal, but I don't recall anything about blood work. I just came in because of the breathing issues, and I haven't had any other tests done.
Doctor: Have you noticed any correlation between your symptoms and specific times of the day, seasons, or activities?
Patient: No, I haven't really noticed any specific time of day or season that seems to trigger it more. It just happens randomly, sometimes when I'm outside, sometimes when I'm at home, even when I'm not doing anything. It's more like my breathing just feels off for no real reason.
Doctor: Have you undergone any recent cardiac evaluations, such as an echocardiogram or ECG, to rule out cardiac causes of dyspnea?
Patient: No, I haven't had any cardiac evaluations like an echocardiogram or ECG. The doctor did some tests, like a chest X-ray and pulmonary function test, which were normal, but I don't think they checked my heart specifically. I just came in because of the breathing issues, and I haven't had any other tests done.

subjective.unit: Chief Complaint: Right knee pain and instability after a week-old injury at a trampoline park.
subjective.citation_text: Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today? Patient: I'm 58 years old, male. I came in because I hurt my right knee a week ago at the trampoline park, and I've been having pain and some trouble walking since then. Doctor: Could you please describe the nature of the pain in your right knee? Is it sharp, dull, or throbbing? Have you noticed any swelling, bruising, or instability in the knee? Patient: The pain is more on the outside of my knee, and it feels like a sharp pain when I put pressure on it. I didn't notice any swelling at first, but now there's some bruising, and my knee feels a little unstable when I walk. It's been pretty uncomfortable, and I've been limping a bit. Doctor: Have you had any prior knee injuries, surgeries, or conditions such as arthritis or ligament tears? Patient: No, I don't have any prior knee injuries or surgeries. I don't have arthritis or any other knee conditions that I'm aware of. This was the first time I ever went to a trampoline park, and that's when I hurt it. Doctor: Could you describe the mechanism of the injury in more detail? For example, did you land awkwardly, twist your knee, or hit the trampoline mat with your knee? Patient: I was jumping on the trampoline, and when I landed, I heard a snap and felt a sudden sharp pain in my right knee. I think I twisted it or maybe landed wrong, but I'm not exactly sure how it happened. It hurt right away, and I couldn't put much weight on it after that. Doctor: Could you describe the range of motion of your right knee and whether you have experienced any locking, clicking, or giving way sensations? Patient: I can bend my knee a little, but it's not much. I can straighten it, but it's uncomfortable. I haven't had any locking or clicking,

Basic information: 35-year-old male with chief complaint of severe back pain radiating down the left leg, affecting mobility and daily activities.

History of present illness: Onset and progression of back pain, with radiation to the left leg, described as an 'electric toothache,' limiting ability to walk, stand, or tie shoes. Use of a cane. Referral from primary care physician. Pain localized to lower back, radiating down the left leg through the hip, along the side of the leg, and to the big toe. Constant pain, exacerbated by standing or walking, rated 8/10 (up to 13/10 at worst). Weakness in both legs, foot dragging when walking.

Past history: History of trauma (fall from roof 30 years ago with suspected fracture, no surgery).

subjective.unit: Chief Complaint: Neck pain since a car accident a week ago.
subjective.citation_text: Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today? Patient: I'm 28, and I'm a guy. I came in because I've been having neck pain since a car accident a week ago. It's been pretty bad, like a seven out of ten, and it hurts when I move my head around. Doctor: Could you please confirm your age, gender, and describe the nature of your neck pain, including any associated symptoms such as numbness, tingling, or weakness? Patient: I'm 28, and I'm a guy. The pain is in the back of my neck, and it's not constant—it gets worse when I move my head. I've had some headaches early on, but nothing else like numbness or tingling. Doctor: Have you undergone any imaging studies or consultations with a specialist for your neck pain since the car accident? Patient: No, I haven't had any imaging studies or gone to see a specialist for this yet. I tried some ibuprofen, and that helped a little, but I didn't go to the hospital because I didn't want the cost. The doctor just did an exam and ordered an MRI now. Doctor: Have you experienced any radiation of pain to your arms, shoulders, or upper back? Have you noticed any changes in your range of motion or any difficulty with daily activities due to the neck pain? Patient: No, the pain just stays in my neck. It's been hard to move my head around, and it hurts when I try to turn my neck from side to side or bend it back. It's been making it tough to do some things normally, but I can still manage most of my daily activities. Doctor: Could you please provide the results of the MRI that was ordered by the doctor? Patient: I haven't had the MRI yet, so I don't have the results. The doctor mentioned they wanted to make sure there wasn't anything more serious, like a concussion or nerve issues,
